1) No experiments have been run, so there is no evidence yet about which design choices matter: modality (RNA, image, or multimodal), profile setting (single vs. multi), encoder type, aggregation, or fusion. 2) config_018 is a central reference point: multimodal, multiprofile with avgpool aggregation and concat fusion, using the simplest encoders (PCA for RNA, ResNet50 for images). It tests whether combining modalities with multiple profiles gives reasonable performance at all. Each later experiment can then change one factor from this baseline, such as dropping a modality, switching to singleprofile, using transformer aggregation, weighted fusion, or a foundation-model encoder (scGPT, ViT-L). That makes the effect of each choice easy to attribute. 3) Starting near the middle of the design space, rather than at an extreme, is the most efficient first step under a limited budget. It has a reasonable chance of performing well, and every follow-up becomes a single-factor test against it.

1) Evidence: there is only one result so far. config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000 + resnet50, avgpool, concat) reached 0.518 accuracy and 0.484 F1. With a single point, we cannot yet tell which design choices matter. 2) Test: config_020 changes only the aggregation from avgpool to a transformer and keeps everything else fixed. This gives a clean one-factor comparison of how the multiple profiles are combined. Learned aggregation is likely one of the larger levers in multiprofile setups, and it is also the more expensive option, so it matters to know early whether it is worth the cost. 3) Why now: a controlled ablation against the existing baseline gives an interpretable result whichever way it goes. Whichever aggregation wins can then be carried forward into later tests of the image encoder (ViT-L), the RNA encoder (scVI or scGPT) and the fusion method. Changing several factors at once would confound the result and waste the limited budget.

1) Evidence: Only two runs exist, both multimodal multiprofile with pca_n2000, resnet50 and concat fusion. The transformer aggregation (config_020) beat avgpool (config_018) by about 2.2 points in accuracy and about 4 points in F1. That is moderate, consistent evidence for transformer aggregation. The encoders and fusion type are still completely untested. 2) This experiment keeps the best setup fixed and swaps only the image encoder from resnet50 to imagenet_vit_l. Changing one factor gives a clean read on whether a larger pretrained image backbone improves the multimodal model. 3) The encoder choice likely matters more than the fusion type, and the image encoder is a major unexplored axis. Testing it next exploits the transformer lead while reducing uncertainty about an important design choice. The result will guide whether later RNA encoder (scVI or scGPT) and fusion comparisons should use ViT-L or ResNet50.

Evidence: all three runs use the pca_n2000 RNA encoder with concat fusion. Within that setup, two single-factor changes each improved results. Switching aggregation from avgpool to transformer gave about +0.022 accuracy (0.518 to 0.540, with ResNet50). Switching the image encoder from ResNet50 to ViT-L gave about +0.059 (0.540 to 0.599, with transformer). The F1 changes track the accuracy changes. Each comparison rests on a single run, so these are early signals only. The RNA encoder is a major design choice and remains completely untested. Experiment: config_050 keeps the current best setup (multiprofile, ViT-L, transformer, concat) and changes only the RNA encoder to scGPT, a pretrained foundation model. This isolates whether the RNA representation matters as much as the image backbone did. Why now: it builds on the strongest configuration found so far, so it also has a good chance of a new best. It also resolves uncertainty about a three-level factor that strongly shapes the remaining search space. That is a more valuable use of one run than testing fusion type, which has only two options and probably a smaller effect.

1) Evidence: Three one-factor changes have each helped. Transformer aggregation beat avgpool by about 2 points (0.540 vs 0.518). ViT-L beat ResNet50 by about 6 points (0.599 vs 0.540). scGPT beat PCA by about 12 points (0.721 vs 0.599), and F1 moved the same way each time. The best configuration so far is config_050 (scGPT, ViT-L, transformer, concat). Fusion is the one major design choice not yet tested: every run so far used concat. 2) Test: config_051 keeps config_050's settings and changes only concat to weighted fusion. This gives a clean estimate of the fusion effect at the strongest setting found so far. 3) Why now: It closes the biggest remaining uncertainty among the multimodal design choices. It also has a reasonable chance of becoming the new best result. Unimodal ablations such as scGPT RNA-only would show how much the image modality contributes, but they are unlikely to beat the current best, so they can come later.

Evidence: switching the RNA encoder from PCA to scGPT gave the largest gain so far (0.599 to 0.721 accuracy, with F1 rising alongside). Image encoder and aggregation choices gave smaller gains of about 0.02 to 0.06, and weighted fusion clearly hurt (0.525). This suggests RNA representation quality may dominate performance, but we do not yet know how much the image branch actually contributes. Test: config_009 is RNA-only with scGPT and transformer aggregation over multiple profiles. It is a direct single-factor ablation of the current best config_050, removing the image modality and fusion while keeping everything else the same. Why now: if it matches or beats 0.72, the remaining budget should shift toward RNA-side choices (encoder, aggregation, single vs. multiprofile) rather than image or fusion variants. If it falls well short, it confirms that multimodal concat adds value and justifies exploiting nearby multimodal variants such as config_038 (scVI) or config_048 (avgpool). Either outcome resolves a high-level design question that steers all later experiments.

1) Evidence: the best result so far is config_050 (scGPT + ViT-L + transformer + concat, 0.721 acc / 0.681 F1). Single swaps suggest ViT-L beats ResNet50, transformer beats avgpool, and concat beats weighted fusion. scGPT beat PCA by about 12 points in the same setting, so the RNA encoder looks like a high-impact choice. However, scVI_n200, one of only three RNA encoders, has never been tested. 2) This experiment keeps the best known settings (ViT-L, transformer, concat) and swaps only the RNA encoder to scVI_n200. The result will show whether scGPT's advantage is specific to scGPT or whether a compact learned latent space is just as good or better. 3) The RNA encoder has shown the largest effect of any choice, and one of its three options is completely unexplored. This controlled test is therefore the best use of one experiment: it reduces uncertainty about an important design choice and could also produce a new best configuration.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_050 (scGPT + ImageNet ViT-L, multiprofile, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) at 0.721 accuracy and 0.681 F1. Several choices already have support. Concat clearly beats weighted fusion (0.721 vs 0.525). scGPT is the strongest RNA encoder tested (it beats PCA and scVI). ViT-L beats ResNet50. Multimodal far exceeds RNA-only (0.721 vs 0.411). Transformer beat avgpool by only a small margin, in a single comparison. The main gap is that profile setting has never been varied: every run so far used multiprofile. 2) Test: config_046 keeps the best encoders and concat fusion but uses singleprofile, which has no aggregation step. This shows whether combining multiple profiles is what drives the gains, or whether single profiles with strong encoders do comparably well. 3) Why now: this is the only major design dimension with no evidence at all. One run anchored to the best configuration gives a clean, one-step comparison, which is the most informative use of a limited budget.

1) Evidence: The best results come from scGPT + ViT-L with concat fusion, at 0.725 for singleprofile and 0.721 for multiprofile transformer. These two are essentially tied, so the profile setting does not yet look decisive. Weighted fusion fell sharply to 0.525 in one run. RNA-only scGPT reached only 0.41, but no image-only model has been run, so we cannot tell how much of the multimodal performance comes from the image branch versus the fusion. 2) Test: A ViT-L image-only singleprofile run is the missing ablation that sits directly next to the best configuration (config_046). It will show whether multimodal fusion gives a real gain over images alone, or whether ViT-L features carry most of the signal. That in turn tells us whether to spend later experiments on RNA encoder and fusion choices or on image-side choices. 3) Value under the budget: the aggregation and fusion variants left around the current best are likely small refinements. This single run resolves a major structural question about the search space instead.

1. Evidence: scGPT with ImageNet ViT-L and concat fusion is clearly the strongest region. Single-profile (config_046, 0.725) and multiprofile with transformer aggregation (config_050, 0.721) perform about the same. The only test of weighted fusion lost about 0.20 accuracy, so concat is the preferred fusion for now. Aggregation is still uncertain in this region. Transformer beat avgpool by about 0.02 accuracy and 0.04 F1, but only in the weaker PCA/ResNet50 setting (config_020 vs config_018). 2. This experiment swaps the transformer for avgpool within the best scGPT + ViT-L + concat setup. It tests whether the transformer's advantage carries over to strong encoders, and whether simpler pooling of multiple profiles can beat the single-profile baseline. 3. It exploits the most promising region while settling a design choice that has been tested only once and only with weak encoders. That makes it both a plausible new best and informative about whether multiprofile aggregation is worth pursuing.

1) Evidence: no experiments have been run, so we have no information about which modality, encoder, aggregation or fusion choice matters. 2) Test: config_030 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI RNA encoder, ResNet50 image encoder, avgpool aggregation, concat fusion) sets a reference point near the middle of the design space. It uses the simplest option on each multimodal axis (avgpool rather than transformer, concat rather than weighted) and standard mid-capacity encoders. 3) Why now: the result can be compared directly with later single-change experiments, such as its unimodal parts (config_005, config_011), its singleprofile version (config_028), a transformer aggregator (config_032), weighted fusion (config_031), or other encoders. That makes each later run an informative test of one factor. Starting from a plausible multimodal configuration also gives a reasonable chance of good accuracy early, rather than spending the first run on a weak unimodal baseline.

1. Evidence: only one run exists. config_030 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI, ResNet50, avgpool, concat) reached 0.520 accuracy and 0.498 F1. With nothing to compare it to, we cannot tell whether the image modality adds anything, and that is the main design question in this search. 2. Test: config_005 keeps everything else the same (scVI, multiprofile, avgpool) and drops the image branch. This makes it a clean single-factor ablation of the image modality against config_030. 3. Why now: the result tells us whether to spend the remaining budget on multimodal configurations (encoder, aggregation and fusion variants) or on stronger RNA-only setups. It also gives a baseline for judging every later change, so it reduces more uncertainty than a single tweak to aggregation or fusion would.

1. Evidence: Adding ResNet50 image features with concat fusion cut validation accuracy from 0.688 (RNA-only, scVI, avgpool) to 0.520, with F1 falling similarly. That is a large drop. We cannot yet tell whether the image modality is unhelpful or whether naive concatenation lets noisy image features swamp the stronger RNA signal. 2. Test: config_031 changes only the fusion, from concat to weighted, keeping the scVI encoder, ResNet50, multiprofile setting and avgpool aggregation. This isolates the effect of fusion. If weighted fusion recovers or beats RNA-only performance, multimodal models stay viable and fusion is a key design choice. If it still underperforms, image features (at least ResNet50) likely hurt, and the remaining budget should go to RNA-only encoder and aggregation choices. 3. Why now: Whether to keep pursuing multimodal models governs most of the remaining search space, which is mostly multimodal. One controlled experiment that resolves this is the most efficient next step.

Evidence: RNA-only scVI with avgpool reached 0.688 accuracy (F1 0.659). Adding ResNet50 image features with the same RNA encoder and aggregation dropped accuracy to about 0.51-0.52 under both concat and weighted fusion. So fusion type is not the cause; the drop points to the ResNet50 image representation, or to multimodal training generally. Test: config_036 keeps everything identical to config_030 (scVI, multiprofile, avgpool, concat) and swaps only ResNet50 for ImageNet ViT-L. This isolates the image-encoder effect inside the multimodal setting. Value: if ViT-L recovers or exceeds the RNA-only result, multimodal fusion is still promising and image-encoder choice is the key factor. If it also falls well below RNA-only, that is strong evidence the image modality adds noise, and the budget should shift toward RNA-only refinements such as transformer aggregation and the scGPT and PCA encoders. Either outcome resolves the largest open uncertainty in this search.

1) Evidence: the only RNA-only run (config_005, scVI + avgpool) reached 0.688 accuracy and 0.659 F1. All three multimodal avgpool runs were far lower, at 0.48–0.52, whether they used concat or weighted fusion and ResNet50 or ViT-L. This consistent gap suggests that adding image features as currently fused hurts performance. The RNA-only branch is the most promising direction. However, every run so far used avgpool, so we know nothing about the transformer aggregator. 2) This experiment keeps the best setup fixed (RNA-only, multiprofile, scVI) and changes only avgpool to transformer. It isolates whether learned attention over multiple profiles improves on simple mean pooling. 3) Why this is the best next run: it exploits the strongest result so far while answering an untested design choice that applies across many configurations. If transformer aggregation helps, it may also explain or rescue the weak multimodal results. If it does not, avgpool becomes the default, and later runs can test the RNA encoder (PCA, scGPT) and single-profile versus multiprofile.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is RNA-only scVI with avgpool (0.688 accuracy, 0.659 F1). Adding images lowered accuracy to about 0.48-0.52 in three runs, across both image encoders and both fusion types. Transformer aggregation collapsed to 0.22. So RNA-only with avgpool is the strongest direction, but every RNA run so far used the scVI encoder. Whether the RNA encoder matters is still completely untested. 2) This run swaps scVI for scGPT and keeps everything else fixed (RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool). That isolates the effect of the RNA encoder within the best-performing setup. 3) It exploits the most promising region while resolving a major uncertainty. If scGPT beats scVI, it becomes the new best and the encoder to carry into any later multimodal runs. If it does not, scVI is confirmed and later runs can test PCA or single-profile versus multiprofile.

1) Evidence: RNA-only scVI with avgpool is the clear leader (0.688 acc, 0.659 F1). Every multimodal run so far is worse, at roughly 0.48–0.52 accuracy. Transformer aggregation performed very poorly (0.224). The RNA encoder choice clearly matters, since scVI beat scGPT by about 0.11 accuracy under the same setup. The PCA_n2000 encoder has never been tested in any setting, so this is the biggest remaining gap on an axis with large effects. 2) config_002 keeps the best-known setup (RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool) and swaps only the encoder to PCA_n2000. This is a clean one-variable comparison against config_005 and config_008, and it tells us whether a simple high-dimensional linear representation matches or beats the learned embeddings. 3) This is both exploitation and exploration. It extends the strongest direction with a real chance of a new best. Its result also decides which encoder should anchor later tests of profile setting (singleprofile) and any further multimodal or fusion runs. Under a limited budget, that makes it more informative than further variants of the weaker multimodal or transformer branches.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is RNA-only scVI with multiprofile avgpool (0.688 accuracy, 0.659 F1). scVI beats both scGPT (0.579) and PCA (0.518), so the encoder choice looks fairly well supported. Adding images has consistently lowered performance to about 0.48–0.52, and transformer aggregation collapsed to 0.224. The profile setting is the main untested factor: every completed run used multiprofile, so we cannot tell whether multiprofile aggregation helps or whether plain single-profile modeling does as well or better. 2. Test: Running config_004 (RNA-only, singleprofile, scVI) changes only the profile setting relative to the current best. It isolates whether pooling multiple profiles adds value. 3. Why this experiment: Profile setting is a top-level design choice that applies to every RNA-only and multimodal configuration, so resolving it is informative across the whole space. Because it pairs this test with the strongest known encoder, it also has a realistic chance of matching or beating the current best. That makes it a good balance of exploration and exploitation for one experiment.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is RNA-only scVI with multiprofile avgpool (0.688 acc, 0.659 F1). Adding images consistently lowered performance. ResNet50 with concat fusion reached 0.520, with weighted fusion 0.512, and ViT-L with concat 0.485. These drops are large and consistent across fusion and image-encoder choices. No image-only model has been tested, so we cannot tell why images hurt. The image features may carry little signal for this task, or the fusion step may be failing to combine two useful modalities. 2. Test: config_011 is an image-only ResNet50 model with multiprofile avgpool. It uses the same profile and aggregation settings as the best RNA runs, so it isolates the standalone predictive value of the image modality. If it scores near chance or well below 0.52, images contribute mostly noise, and the remaining budget should go to RNA-only refinements. If it scores reasonably well, the failure lies in fusion, and other multimodal setups (e.g., transformer aggregation or different RNA encoders) deserve testing. 3. Why now: About two-thirds of the untested space is multimodal. Knowing whether images carry signal at all decides whether that whole region is worth exploring, which makes this the most informative use of the next experiment.

1) Evidence: Multiprofile RNA-only with avgpool is the strongest direction so far. scvi_n200 reaches 0.688, scGPT 0.579 and PCA 0.518. Every multimodal run lands near the image-only level (about 0.48-0.52). The one transformer-aggregation run (scvi_n200, RNA-only) collapsed to 0.224 accuracy and 0.184 F1, but that is a single data point. It could reflect a general weakness of transformer aggregation or a problem specific to scVI embeddings or that one run. Transformer aggregation also appears in about half of the remaining configurations, so this uncertainty matters. 2) Test: scGPT RNA-only with transformer aggregation changes only the RNA encoder relative to the failed run. Its avgpool counterpart (config_008, 0.579) gives a clean reference. A similar collapse would show transformer aggregation is broadly harmful, and the many transformer variants could be deprioritized. Performance near or above 0.58 would show the failure was encoder-specific, keeping transformer aggregation in play. 3) Why now: this is a cheap, well-controlled comparison in the strongest setting (RNA-only, multiprofile). It resolves a high-leverage design question that determines how much of the remaining budget goes to transformer configurations, rather than adding another multimodal point to a pattern that is already fairly consistent.

1) No experiments have been run, so we have no evidence yet on which design choices matter: modality, profile setting, encoders, aggregation or fusion. 2) This config is a central multimodal anchor. It uses the simple avgpool aggregation and concat fusion, a mid-sized learned RNA embedding (scVI) and a strong pretrained image encoder (ViT-L). It tests whether a reasonable full multimodal, multi-profile pipeline performs well, giving a reference point. 3) Starting near the middle of the design space is the most budget-efficient opening. Each later experiment can change one factor from this anchor (RNA-only or image-only, single profile, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion, other encoders) and isolate its effect. A plain unimodal baseline would only inform one corner of the space.

Evidence: only one experiment has run. Multimodal, multiprofile, scVI plus ViT-L, avgpool and concat reached 0.706 accuracy and 0.667 F1, so we have no baseline to judge what drives that result. Test: config_005 keeps everything the same (scVI, multiprofile, avgpool) but removes the image branch. This directly measures how much the image modality adds over RNA alone. Why now: multimodal vs. unimodal is the most important high-level choice and determines how the rest of the search space should be prioritized. If RNA alone nearly matches 0.706, later budget should go to RNA encoders and aggregation. If accuracy drops clearly, image encoder and fusion choices deserve more attention. Changing a single variable makes the comparison easy to interpret.

1) Evidence and uncertainty: The multimodal model (scVI + ViT-L, avgpool, concat) reached 0.706 accuracy and 0.667 F1. The matched RNA-only model reached 0.650 accuracy and 0.628 F1. With the encoders and avgpool aggregation held the same, adding image features was associated with about a 5.6-point accuracy gain, and F1 agreed. This is one pair of runs, so it is promising rather than conclusive. Aggregation (avgpool vs transformer) has not been tested at all, and it applies to every multiprofile configuration. 2) What this tests: config_038 changes only the aggregation, from avgpool to transformer, in the best configuration so far. It is a clean one-factor comparison showing whether learned attention over a profile set beats simple averaging. 3) Why this is the best next experiment: It exploits the strongest current direction while resolving a design choice that affects half of the remaining search space. The result will guide later tests of encoders and fusion, whichever way it comes out. Image-only ablations or encoder swaps are informative, but they are less likely to improve the best result and less likely to change which configurations we test next.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is multimodal scVI + ViT-L with avgpool and concat fusion (acc 0.706, F1 0.667). It beats RNA-only with the same encoder and aggregation (0.650), which suggests the image modality adds value. Transformer aggregation did much worse (0.542), so avgpool looks like the better aggregation for now. Fusion strategy is completely untested: concat is the only fusion method tried. 2) This run keeps everything from the best configuration fixed and changes only concat to weighted fusion. That isolates the effect of fusion, a design choice that applies to every multimodal configuration. 3) Under a limited budget, a one-factor change next to the current best both exploits the strongest direction and resolves a key open question. Whichever fusion wins can then be used in later tests of the RNA encoders (scGPT, PCA) and the image encoder (ResNet50).

1) Evidence so far: the best run is config_036 (multimodal, scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, concat; acc 0.706, F1 0.667). It beats the matched RNA-only baseline (0.650), which suggests images add value. Within this backbone, switching to transformer aggregation (0.542) or weighted fusion (0.632) clearly hurt, so avgpool + concat is the current working recipe. The RNA encoder choice is still completely unexplored: only scvi_n200 has been tested, and RNA alone already carries most of the signal. 2) This run keeps the best recipe fixed (multimodal, multiprofile, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, concat) and swaps only the RNA encoder to scGPT. That gives a clean one-factor comparison of a foundation-model RNA embedding against scVI. 3) It is the best use of the next experiment because it exploits the strongest known recipe while resolving a major open design choice. The result will guide whether later runs should centre on scGPT or scVI before probing the image encoder (resnet50) or single-profile settings.

Evidence: in multimodal multiprofile runs, avgpool clearly beat transformer aggregation (0.706 vs 0.542), and concat beat weighted fusion (0.706 vs 0.632). scGPT slightly outperformed scVI (0.713 vs 0.706, F1 0.695 vs 0.667). Multimodal also beat RNA-only (0.706 vs 0.650). However, every multimodal run so far has used imagenet_vit_l, so the image encoder is a major design choice with no evidence at all. This experiment keeps the best-known setup (scGPT, multiprofile, avgpool, concat) and swaps only the image encoder to resnet50. That isolates the effect of the image encoder. It is the best use of the budget because it closes the largest remaining gap in an important axis, within the most promising region. It either confirms vit_l or finds a better image backbone.

1) Evidence: Multimodal models with ViT-L, avgpool and concat fusion are clearly the best so far: scGPT reached 0.713 accuracy (F1 0.695) and scVI reached 0.706. Swapping in ResNet50, transformer aggregation or weighted fusion each lowered performance, though each of those comparisons rests on a single run. Every experiment so far used multiprofile, so the profile setting is a major design choice with no evidence at all. 2) Test: config_046 keeps the best setup (scGPT, ViT-L, concat) but uses singleprofile. Comparing it with config_048 isolates whether multiprofile with avgpool actually helps, or whether a simpler single-profile model does as well or better. 3) Why now: This targets the largest untested factor and stays close to the current best region, so it may still score well. Its result also decides whether the rest of the budget should go to multiprofile or singleprofile variants.

1) Evidence: The best results come from multiprofile + avgpool + concat with the ImageNet ViT-L image encoder (scGPT 0.713 accuracy, scVI 0.706). Two choices look clear so far. ViT-L beat ResNet50 by a wide margin (0.713 vs 0.530), and multiprofile avgpool beat singleprofile (0.713 vs 0.507). Avgpool beat transformer and concat beat weighted, but each of those rests on a single comparison. RNA-only scVI reached 0.650, below the 0.706 of its multimodal counterpart. The open question is how much each modality contributes. The two RNA encoders perform almost the same, which suggests the ViT-L image features may drive most of the performance. 2) This experiment tests ViT-L image-only with multiprofile avgpool, the best aggregation found so far. If it comes close to 0.71, fusion and RNA-encoder choices matter little, and the remaining budget should go to image-side and aggregation design. If it is well below, multimodal fusion is confirmed as essential, and tuning RNA encoders and fusion is justified. 3) A modality ablation resolves the most important open design decision, whether to use RNA, image or both. That tells us more than another small variant near the current best, such as the PCA encoder or weighted fusion, which would likely shift accuracy only marginally.

1) Evidence: multiprofile + avgpool + concat with the ViT-L image encoder is the strongest template so far. scGPT scored 0.713 accuracy (F1 0.695) and scVI scored 0.706 (F1 0.667). The alternatives each lost clearly in their single head-to-head tests: transformer aggregation, weighted fusion, the ResNet50 image encoder and single-profile input. Multimodal also beat RNA-only (0.650) and image-only (0.411). The RNA encoder is now the main unresolved choice, because scGPT and scVI are nearly tied and PCA (pca_n2000) has never been tested. 2) This experiment runs PCA in the best-known template, completing the RNA-encoder comparison with everything else held fixed. It will show whether the choice of pretrained RNA embedding matters or whether a simple PCA baseline does as well or better. 3) It has a realistic chance of beating the current best while also resolving uncertainty about a whole design factor. That makes it a better use of the limited budget than further one-off ablations of components that have already lost once.

1) Evidence: The two best runs are scGPT and scVI, each with ViT-L, avgpool and concat (0.713 and 0.706). The other design choices are supported by only one comparison each. Weighted fusion fell to 0.632 from 0.706, but this was tested only with scVI. Some effects look clearer. ViT-L beat ResNet50 for scGPT. Multiprofile beat singleprofile. Multimodal beat both unimodal baselines for scVI. 2) Test: config_049 changes only the fusion to weighted while keeping the current best scGPT/ViT-L/avgpool setup. This shows whether concat's advantage holds across RNA encoders or whether weighted fusion works better with scGPT embeddings. 3) Why now: the fusion conclusion rests on a single run, and this experiment sits right next to the best configuration. It either strengthens a key design decision or reveals an encoder-fusion interaction, while still having a reasonable chance of a new best. Transformer aggregation lost much more clearly (about 0.16 lower), so that axis is a lower priority.

1) No experiments have been run, so there is no evidence about which design choices matter. That covers modality, single vs. multi-profile, RNA encoder, image encoder, aggregation and fusion. 2) Config_030 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI-200, ResNet50, avgpool, concat) uses a middle-of-the-road setting on every factor: a compact learned RNA embedding, a standard image backbone, the simplest aggregation and the simplest fusion. It sets a baseline for the full multimodal pipeline, from which each factor can be tested by changing one thing at a time. Examples are switching to RNA-only (config_005) or image-only (config_011), single-profile (config_028), transformer aggregation (config_032), weighted fusion (config_031), or a different encoder (config_042 or config_036). 3) A unimodal baseline such as config_001 could tell us about only one branch. This multimodal anchor touches every design dimension, is plausibly strong, and lets the next few experiments act as clean ablations. That makes it the most efficient use of a limited budget.

1. Evidence: Only one run exists. Multimodal scVI + ResNet50 with avgpool and concat fusion reached 0.532 accuracy and 0.516 F1. One run gives no reference point, so we cannot yet tell which design choices drive performance. 2. What this tests: config_005 keeps the scVI encoder, multiprofile setting and avgpool aggregation, and removes only the image branch. This single-factor ablation shows whether the ResNet50 image features add anything over RNA alone. 3. Why now: Whether to fuse modalities at all is the most basic decision in the search space. The answer decides whether the budget should go to multimodal variants (image encoder, fusion type, aggregation) or to RNA-only refinement. It is more informative than tuning a secondary factor before we know if multimodality helps.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: Only two runs exist, both using scvi_n200 with avgpool aggregation. RNA-only had slightly higher accuracy (0.542 vs 0.532). Multimodal concat had noticeably higher F1 (0.516 vs 0.483). This hints that adding the image modality helps balanced class performance, but the accuracy gap is too small to read much into. Aggregation is untested: every run so far used avgpool. 2. What this tests: config_032 keeps everything from config_030 the same (multimodal, scvi_n200, resnet50, concat) and swaps only avgpool for transformer. This isolates the effect of the aggregation method. It does so in the multimodal setting, which has the strongest supporting F1 evidence. 3. Why it is the best next use of budget: Aggregation affects every multiprofile configuration, so resolving it early narrows the remaining search space a lot. Testing it on the more promising multimodal setting also gives a reasonable chance of a new best result, balancing learning with performance.

1. Evidence: Transformer aggregation lifted the multimodal scVI+ResNet50 concat model from 0.532 to 0.713 accuracy, with F1 rising from 0.516 to 0.695. Under avgpool, RNA-only (0.542) roughly matched multimodal (0.532), so it is unclear whether images add anything. 2. Test: config_006 is the RNA-only scVI multiprofile model with transformer aggregation. It is the direct ablation of the best run. If it nears 0.71, the gain comes mainly from the aggregation and images add little. If it stays well below, the image modality contributes under transformer aggregation. 3. Why now: Whether images help decides how much of the remaining budget should go to image-encoder and fusion choices (ViT-L vs ResNet50, weighted vs concat) or to RNA encoders with transformer aggregation. One run resolves this, which is a better use of budget than a local tweak to the current best.

Evidence: the best result so far is multimodal scVI + ResNet50 with transformer aggregation and concat fusion (0.713 accuracy, 0.695 F1). Swapping in avgpool drops this to 0.532. RNA-only with a transformer is poor (0.435), below RNA-only with avgpool (0.542). So the transformer gain appears only when image features are present, but we cannot yet tell whether it comes from the image modality itself or from combining the two. Test: image-only ResNet50 with multiprofile transformer aggregation isolates the image contribution under the best aggregation setting. If it approaches 0.71, images drive performance, and later experiments should focus on image encoders (e.g., ViT-L) and aggregation rather than RNA encoders or fusion. If it falls well short, combining modalities is what matters, and fusion type (weighted vs concat) and RNA encoder choice deserve the next experiments. Why now: one run resolves which modality drives the leading result. That guides how the remaining budget is split between image-side and RNA/fusion-side exploration, which is more informative than a single small tweak to config_032.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_032 (multimodal, scVI, ResNet50, transformer, concat) at 0.713 accuracy and 0.695 F1. It is far ahead of the avgpool multimodal run (0.532) and the unimodal baselines (0.43–0.54). Transformer aggregation with multimodal fusion therefore looks strongly promising. The image encoder has only been tested with ResNet50, and image-only ResNet50 was weak (0.494), so image representation quality is a major open uncertainty. 2. Test: config_038 keeps the winning setup fixed and swaps only ResNet50 for ImageNet ViT-L. This isolates whether a stronger image backbone improves the best pipeline. 3. Budget: It exploits the strong transformer-multimodal direction while answering one important, untested design question. A backbone swap plausibly affects performance more than the fusion choice (concat vs. weighted), so it is the most informative single-variable extension. Fusion type and RNA encoder can be tested next.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_032 (multimodal, scVI, ResNet50, transformer, concat) at 0.713 accuracy and 0.695 F1. Under concat fusion, the transformer clearly beat avgpool (0.713 vs 0.532) and ResNet50 beat ViT-L (0.713 vs 0.639). Multimodal also beat both single-modality baselines. The main uncertainty is fusion: weighted fusion has never been tested, so all multimodal conclusions so far depend on concat. 2. Test: config_033 changes only concat to weighted fusion in the best configuration. Any difference can therefore be attributed to the fusion method. 3. Value: This is a low-risk extension of the leading configuration that could beat it, and it resolves an entire untested design dimension in one run. That result will guide whether later multimodal runs (e.g., testing PCA or scGPT RNA encoders) should use concat or weighted fusion.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_032 (scVI + ResNet50 + transformer + concat, 0.713 acc / 0.695 F1). Three single-factor changes from it all performed worse. Swapping in ViT-L gave 0.639, weighted fusion gave 0.632, and avgpool aggregation gave 0.532. Multimodal transformer also clearly beats the unimodal runs. The RNA encoder is the one axis never varied. scVI is the only RNA encoder tested in any setting, so whether it is a good choice is the largest remaining uncertainty. 2) Test: config_044 keeps the winning setup (ResNet50, transformer, concat) and swaps only scVI for scGPT. Any difference can therefore be credited to the RNA representation. 3) Why now: This closes the last untested single-factor comparison around the current best. It could find a stronger configuration if the foundation-model embeddings help. If scGPT underperforms, that strengthens confidence that scVI is the right choice before testing PCA or further combinations.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_032 (scVI + ResNet50 + transformer + concat, 0.713 acc, 0.695 F1). Each component has been varied once around it. Avgpool dropped accuracy to 0.532, ViT-L to 0.639, weighted fusion to 0.632 and scGPT to 0.224. The scGPT drop shows the RNA encoder is a very high-impact choice. The third option, PCA (pca_n2000), has never been tested in any setting. 2) This experiment changes only the RNA encoder to PCA and keeps the best image, aggregation and fusion settings. It directly shows whether scVI is truly the best RNA representation or whether a simpler, higher-dimensional PCA input does as well or better. 3) The RNA encoder has shown the largest effect of any factor, and one of its three options is still unexplored. A one-change comparison against the current best is interpretable, and it could also produce a new best. That makes it a better use of budget than further fusion or image-encoder variants, which already look inferior. Single-profile settings are the next untested question after this.

1) Evidence: Every completed experiment used the multiprofile setting. Within it, the best configuration so far is config_032 (scVI + ResNet50 + transformer + concat, 0.713 accuracy, 0.695 F1). That run clearly beat the avgpool version (0.532), weighted fusion (0.632), the ViT-L image encoder (0.639), the PCA RNA encoder (0.507) and the scGPT RNA encoder (0.224). It also beat the unimodal baselines. So the encoders, aggregation and fusion choices now have reasonable evidence. The profile setting is completely untested. 2) This experiment: config_028 keeps config_032's strongest components (scVI, ResNet50, concat) but switches to the single-profile setting, which has no aggregation. It directly tests whether multiprofile aggregation itself drives the gain, or whether a simpler single-profile model is competitive. The avgpool result (0.532) suggests aggregation choice matters a lot, so a single-profile baseline is needed to read that effect correctly. 3) Why now: further tweaks to fusion or encoders are unlikely to beat config_032 given the current evidence. Testing this untouched, high-level design choice removes the largest remaining uncertainty while staying anchored to the best known configuration.

1) No experiments have been run yet, so we have no evidence on any design choice: modality (RNA, image, or multimodal), single- vs multi-profile input, encoder type, aggregation, or fusion. 2) config_018 is a simple, central multimodal anchor. It uses basic encoders (PCA RNA, ResNet50 image), simple avgpool aggregation and concat fusion, and sits on the multimodal/multiprofile branch that likely has the highest ceiling. Its result sets a baseline from which single-factor changes can be tested next: removing a modality (config_002, config_011), switching to single-profile (config_016), swapping encoders (scVI/scGPT, ViT-L), and trying transformer aggregation or weighted fusion. 3) Under a limited budget, a mid-complexity anchor pays off both ways. It is a reasonable chance at strong performance, and it serves as the shared reference point that makes later one-factor comparisons interpretable. A unimodal or most-complex starting point would leave more confounded factors.

1. Evidence: Only one experiment has been run. config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000 + resnet50, avgpool, concat) reached 0.535 accuracy and 0.519 F1. With one data point, we cannot tell how much each component contributes. 2. What this tests: config_002 is a controlled ablation that changes one thing. It keeps the same RNA encoder, multiprofile setting and avgpool aggregation, but removes the image branch. This directly measures whether adding resnet50 images to concat fusion helps beyond RNA alone. 3. Why now: Modality is the most basic design choice in the space. If RNA-only matches config_018, the image encoder and fusion choices probably matter little, and later budget should go to RNA encoders (scvi, scgpt) and aggregation. If RNA-only is clearly worse, multimodal is confirmed as a real benefit, and later experiments can focus on image encoder (vit_l), aggregation and fusion. Either result cleanly prunes a large part of the search space.

1. Evidence: Two experiments share the same RNA encoder (pca_n2000), multiprofile setting and avgpool aggregation. Adding ResNet50 image features with concat fusion lowered validation accuracy from 0.639 (RNA-only) to 0.535, and F1 fell similarly (0.620 to 0.519). The open question is why. Either concatenation lets weaker or noisier image features dilute the RNA signal, or the image modality simply adds no useful information here. 2. Test: config_019 changes only one thing, swapping concat for weighted fusion. If accuracy recovers to or above the RNA-only baseline, fusion strategy is the bottleneck and the multimodal half of the search space stays worth exploring. If it stays near 0.535, image features are likely harmful in general, and the search should shift toward RNA-only variants such as other RNA encoders or transformer aggregation. 3. Why now: Fusion choice affects about half of the remaining configurations. A clean one-variable comparison with the existing multimodal run is the most efficient way to decide whether multimodal models deserve more of the limited budget.

1) Evidence: RNA-only (PCA, multiprofile, avgpool) is the best result so far at 0.639 accuracy and 0.620 F1. Both multimodal runs with ResNet50 did worse (0.535 and 0.512) under either fusion. So RNA appears to be the main source of signal, and these ResNet50 image features have not helped. The RNA encoder, which may matter a lot, has only been tested with PCA. 2) This run keeps the best setup (RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool) and swaps PCA for scGPT. It tests whether a pretrained foundation-model RNA embedding beats PCA. 3) Since RNA carries most of the signal, the RNA encoder is the design choice most likely to move accuracy, and the result will guide which encoder to use in later multimodal runs. This is a better use of the budget than more fusion or aggregation variants built on the weak image branch.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is RNA-only PCA with multiprofile avgpool (0.639 acc, 0.620 F1). Adding ResNet50 images lowered performance under both concat (0.535) and weighted fusion (0.512), and scGPT was much weaker than PCA (0.435). Every multiprofile run so far used avgpool, so we do not know whether the aggregation method matters. 2. Test: config_003 changes only avgpool to transformer on the strongest baseline. This isolates the effect of aggregation and gives a clean, single-factor comparison. 3. Why now: Aggregation affects every multiprofile configuration, including all the remaining multimodal and image variants. Resolving it on the best-performing branch is both a reasonable exploitation step and a large reduction in uncertainty for future choices. It is a better use of the next run than testing image backbones or the scVI encoder first, since those will benefit from knowing which aggregator to use.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is RNA-only with PCA-2000, multiprofile and avgpool (acc 0.639, F1 0.620). The RNA encoder matters a lot: scGPT in the same setting scored about 0.20 lower. Adding ResNet50 images lowered performance (0.535 concat, 0.512 weighted), and transformer aggregation did worse than avgpool (0.537). The third RNA encoder, scVI-200, has not been tested at all. 2) Test: config_005 swaps only the encoder to scVI-200 and keeps every other setting from the best configuration. This isolates whether scVI can match or beat PCA. 3) Why now: The encoder is the factor with the largest observed effect, and scVI is its largest remaining unknown. The result could raise the best score directly, and it also decides which RNA encoder should carry into later multimodal and profile-setting experiments. That makes it more valuable than testing secondary choices such as fusion type or image backbone under an encoder that may not be the best.

1) Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is RNA-only PCA with avgpool on multiprofile input (0.639 accuracy, 0.620 F1). Swapping in other RNA encoders (scVI 0.494, scGPT 0.435), using transformer aggregation (0.537) or adding ResNet50 images (0.535 and 0.512) all did worse. Every run so far used multiprofile input, so we do not yet know whether multiprofile aggregation helps at all. The transformer drop hints that aggregation may add noise. 2) What this tests: config_001 runs the winning RNA-only PCA setup on single-profile input. It isolates the profile-setting effect, a major design axis with no data yet. 3) Why it is the best next use of budget: It cleanly answers a first-order question about the current best configuration. It also has a realistic chance of becoming the new best, which matters for exploitation. Whether to probe the image modality (for example image-only or ViT-L multimodal) can follow once the RNA baseline's profile setting is understood.

Evidence: pca_n2000 is clearly the strongest RNA encoder. It beats scVI and scGPT, and multiprofile avgpool (0.639) is the best result so far. Adding ResNet50 images lowered accuracy with both concat (0.535) and weighted fusion (0.512). The open question is why: is the image modality uninformative, or is ResNet50 a poor image encoder for this task? The other image encoder, imagenet_vit_l, has never been tested in any setting. This experiment keeps everything from the best multimodal setup (pca_n2000, multiprofile, avgpool, concat, which beat weighted) and swaps only the image encoder. That isolates whether image-encoder choice drives the multimodal penalty. If ViT-L closes or reverses the gap with RNA-only, the multimodal ViT-L configurations become worth exploring. If it does not, the image modality likely adds little, and the remaining budget can go to the RNA-only side. Either outcome resolves a major uncertainty, and the run also has a realistic chance of producing a new best, so it serves both exploration and exploitation.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_024 (PCA + ViT-L, avgpool, concat; acc 0.688, F1 0.659). It beats RNA-only PCA avgpool (0.639). By contrast, PCA + ResNet50 multimodal runs scored below RNA-only (0.512-0.535), so the gain depends strongly on which image encoder is used. Two patterns look consistent but rest on only one or two comparisons each: avgpool beat transformer aggregation for RNA-only, and concat beat weighted fusion with ResNet50. No image-only model has been tested, so it is unclear whether ViT-L image features carry most of the signal by themselves or whether the gain comes from combining them with RNA. 2) Test: Image-only ViT-L with multiprofile avgpool isolates the image branch under the best-performing aggregation. If it scores near 0.69, the image representation is the main driver, and RNA adds little at the current fusion settings. If it scores clearly lower, the two modalities are complementary, and further fusion and aggregation tuning on PCA + ViT-L (e.g., config_025 or config_026) is well justified. 3) Why now: This single run settles the attribution question behind the main design choice, whether to invest in multimodal fusion or in image encoders. That makes it more informative under the limited budget than a small fusion or aggregation tweak to config_024, which the current trends suggest is unlikely to give a large improvement.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is image-only ViT-L with multiprofile avgpool (0.725 acc, 0.685 F1). Adding PCA RNA via concat lowered it to 0.688, and ResNet50-based multimodal runs were much weaker (0.51 to 0.54). This points to the ViT-L image branch as the main source of performance. Aggregation is still uncertain: transformer aggregation underperformed avgpool once, for PCA RNA (0.537 vs 0.639). That is a single experiment on a different modality, so it may not transfer to image features. 2) Test: Swapping avgpool for transformer aggregation on the leading image-only ViT-L configuration isolates whether learned multi-profile aggregation helps the strongest branch. 3) Why now: This exploits the most promising direction while settling a key design choice. If transformer aggregation helps, it could raise the best accuracy and would change which multimodal variants (e.g. config_026 and config_027) are worth running. If it hurts, it confirms that avgpool generalizes across modalities, and later experiments can focus on fusion and RNA-encoder choices.

1. Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been run yet, so nothing is known about which design choices matter: modality, single vs. multiprofile, RNA encoder, image encoder, aggregation or fusion. 2. What this tests: config_036 is a central anchor point. It is multimodal and multiprofile, uses a moderately strong RNA encoder (scVI), a strong pretrained image encoder (ViT-L), simple avgpool aggregation and the simplest fusion (concat). Its result gives a plausible high-performing reference, though that is an expectation rather than evidence. 3. Why it is the best next step: Because the configuration sits in the middle of the design space, later runs can each change one factor from it. Examples include dropping a modality (config_005, config_014), switching to singleprofile (config_034), changing to transformer aggregation (config_038), weighted fusion (config_037) or other encoders (config_030, config_048). Each comparison then isolates one design choice. This makes efficient use of a limited budget while starting from a region likely to score well.

1. Evidence: Only one experiment is complete. The multimodal model (scVI RNA + ViT-L image, multiprofile avgpool, concat fusion) reached 0.332 accuracy and 0.315 F1. With no comparison point, we cannot yet tell whether the image branch adds anything. That is the most basic open question in the design space, and it affects how the rest of the budget should be spent. 2. Test: config_005 keeps the RNA encoder, profile setting and aggregation the same and removes only the image modality. The result will show directly how much the image branch contributes, on both accuracy and F1. 3. Why now: A clean single-factor modality ablation is the highest-value question at this sparse stage. If RNA-only matches the multimodal model, later experiments should focus on RNA encoders and aggregation. If it falls clearly short, image encoders and fusion strategies deserve more of the budget. Questions like fusion type or transformer aggregation are second-order until this is settled.

1. Evidence: with the same scVI-n200 encoder, multiprofile setting and avgpool aggregation, RNA-only reached 0.653 accuracy and 0.628 F1. Adding ImageNet ViT-L image features with concat fusion dropped this to 0.332 accuracy and 0.315 F1. It is unclear whether the image modality is unhelpful or whether concat fusion is the problem, for example high-dimensional ViT features swamping the RNA signal. 2. Test: config_037 is identical to config_036 except it uses weighted fusion, so it isolates the fusion choice. If weighted fusion recovers or beats RNA-only performance, concat was the bottleneck and multimodal search remains promising. If it stays low, the image features themselves are likely the issue. 3. Value: fusion type affects every multimodal configuration, which is most of the remaining space. One controlled comparison here will guide many later choices more than testing another RNA encoder or aggregation would.

1. Evidence: RNA-only scVI with avgpool (config_005) reached 0.653 accuracy. Adding ImageNet ViT-L image features with the same RNA encoder and aggregation sharply reduced accuracy, to 0.332 with concat fusion and 0.494 with weighted fusion. F1 followed the same pattern. Weighted fusion was clearly better than concat, which suggests the model does better when it can down-weight the image branch. The open question is whether image data hurts in general or whether the ViT-L features are the problem. 2. Test: config_031 keeps everything the same as config_037 (multiprofile, scVI, avgpool, weighted fusion) and changes only the image encoder to ResNet50. This isolates the image-encoder effect within the better fusion strategy. 3. Why now: whether to keep pursuing multimodal models at all is the most consequential design decision, and it should be resolved before spending more budget on smaller choices like aggregation or RNA encoder. If ResNet50 multimodal approaches or beats RNA-only, the image branch is worth keeping with a better encoder. If it also underperforms, that is strong evidence to focus remaining experiments on RNA-only refinements such as transformer aggregation or scGPT.

1) Evidence: RNA-only with scvi_n200 and avgpool is clearly the best result so far (acc 0.653, F1 0.628). All three multimodal runs scored much lower (0.33–0.52), so adding image features appears to hurt in the current setup, especially with concat fusion. Aggregation is still a major unknown, because only avgpool has been tried in any run. 2) This experiment keeps the best setup (RNA-only, multiprofile, scvi_n200) and changes only the aggregation from avgpool to transformer. That isolates whether learned attention over multiple profiles beats simple averaging. 3) It is the best next step because it extends the strongest direction while answering an untested design question with a clean one-factor comparison. The answer also guides later choices, since the aggregation result can carry over to other RNA encoders and to any revisited multimodal setups. Comparing RNA encoders (scGPT, PCA) is the natural follow-up.

1. Evidence: RNA-only models with scvi_n200 clearly lead (0.653 with avgpool, 0.678 with transformer). Every multimodal run scored much lower (0.33 to 0.52), so adding images has hurt so far. Transformer aggregation gave a small but consistent gain in both accuracy and F1. The biggest untested design choice is the RNA encoder, since only scvi_n200 has been tried. 2. Test: config_009 keeps the strongest setup (RNA-only, multiprofile, transformer) and swaps in scGPT. This isolates whether a pretrained foundation-model encoder beats scVI. 3. Why now: it explores a key unknown while staying in the best-performing region. If scGPT wins, it sets a new best and changes which encoder later multimodal runs should use. If it loses, it supports scvi_n200 as the default and narrows the search.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: RNA-only models are clearly strongest so far (scVI with transformer 0.678 and with avgpool 0.653). All multimodal runs used avgpool and did much worse (0.33-0.52). Weighted fusion beat concat by a wide margin, and resnet50 with weighted fusion (config_031, 0.520) was the best multimodal run. For RNA-only, transformer aggregation beat avgpool. So it is unclear whether multimodal models are poor because adding images hurts, or because avgpool handles multiple profiles badly. 2. What this tests: config_033 keeps everything from the best multimodal run (scVI, resnet50, weighted fusion) and changes only the aggregation to transformer. That isolates whether transformer aggregation can recover multimodal performance toward or above the RNA-only level. 3. Why this is the best use of the budget: the result decides whether the remaining multimodal transformer configurations are worth exploring. If accuracy stays well below the RNA-only runs, later experiments should focus on RNA-only variants or on image-only baselines to check how much signal the images carry.

1. Evidence: RNA-only models clearly lead, at 0.64-0.68 accuracy, while every multimodal run is far lower, at 0.33-0.52. Adding images currently hurts, so further multimodal tuning is low-value for now. Within RNA-only, transformer aggregation beat avgpool for scVI (0.678 vs 0.653, supported by F1). scVI also beat scGPT under transformer (0.678 vs 0.639). The pca_n2000 encoder has never been tested, so the RNA encoder choice, a major design decision, is still only partly mapped. 2. Test: config_003 keeps the best-performing setup (RNA-only, multiprofile, transformer) and swaps in pca_n2000. This isolates the encoder effect against config_006 and config_009 and checks whether a simple high-dimensional PCA baseline matches or beats the learned embeddings. 3. Why now: it exploits the strongest known direction while resolving the largest remaining uncertainty that could change the best configuration. It is more likely to improve on the current best than image-only or more multimodal runs. Single-profile baselines can be tested next once the encoder ranking is clearer.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: RNA-only models clearly lead. The best is scvi_n200 with transformer aggregation (0.678 accuracy, 0.646 F1), and scvi_n200 has beaten both scgpt and pca_n2000. All four multimodal runs fell far below RNA-only (0.33–0.52), so adding images currently hurts. However, every run so far has used the multiprofile setting, so we have no evidence on whether aggregating multiple profiles helps at all. 2. What this tests: config_004 is the singleprofile counterpart of the best RNA-only setup, keeping the scvi_n200 encoder fixed. It directly measures how much the multiprofile setting, and with it the aggregation step, contributes. Comparing it with config_005 (avgpool) and config_006 (transformer) separates the effect of using multiple profiles from the effect of the aggregation method. 3. Why it is the best use of budget: profile setting is a top-level design choice that applies to every model family, and it is completely unexplored. One run in the strongest region of the search space resolves this uncertainty. That is more useful than further multimodal variants, which consistently underperform, or than small encoder swaps.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: RNA-only models are clearly strongest. The best is scvi_n200 with transformer aggregation (0.678 accuracy, 0.646 F1), followed by scvi avgpool (0.653). Every multimodal run underperforms these, from 0.33 to 0.52 accuracy. However, no image-only model has been tested, so we do not know why fusion hurts. The image features might carry little signal on their own. Alternatively, the fusion step might be dragging down a usable image signal. 2. What this tests: config_011 runs the image-only branch with resnet50, multiprofile and avgpool. This is the image encoder and aggregation used in the best multimodal run so far (config_031, 0.52), so the comparison is direct. It measures how much signal the image modality has by itself. 3. Why now: this closes the largest unexplored axis (image-only) with one controlled run. If image-only accuracy is near chance, further multimodal and fusion experiments are low value and the budget should go to RNA-only refinement. If it is reasonably strong, the fusion design is the bottleneck and is worth more experiments.

1. Evidence: No experiments have been run, so nothing is known yet about any design choice: modality, single- vs multi-profile, RNA encoder, image encoder, aggregation or fusion. 2. What it tests: config_030 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI RNA encoder, ResNet50 image encoder, avgpool aggregation, concat fusion) is a central, moderately complex anchor. It uses both modalities and multiple profiles, which are plausible sources of gain. It pairs mid-range encoders (scVI rather than PCA or scGPT, ResNet50 rather than ViT-L) with the simplest options for aggregation and fusion. Its result sets a strong reference point. Later one-factor-at-a-time changes can then measure the effect of each choice: single-profile, unimodal ablations, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion, or swapping encoders. 3. Why now: Starting from a central, likely competitive configuration balances exploitation, since it has a reasonable chance of good accuracy and F1, with exploration, since it gives a clean baseline for the most informative follow-up ablations under a limited budget.

1. Evidence: we have only one result so far. config_030 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI-200 + ResNet50, avgpool, concat) reached 0.520 accuracy and 0.479 F1. With a single data point, we cannot yet tell which design choices drive performance. The most basic open question is whether the image branch adds anything beyond RNA. 2. Test: config_005 keeps everything else identical (scVI-200, multiprofile, avgpool) and removes only the image modality, so it is a clean one-factor ablation. If RNA-only performs about as well as config_030, image features from ResNet50 add little. In that case the search should focus on RNA encoders and aggregation rather than image encoders and fusion. If accuracy drops clearly, that supports multimodal fusion and justifies spending budget on image encoder and fusion variants. 3. Why now: this choice decides how the remaining budget is spent across the largest group of configurations (the multimodal ones). 1. Evidence: Adding ResNet50 image features to the scVI RNA model (config_030, acc 0.520) did not beat RNA-only scVI with avgpool (config_005, acc 0.520), and F1 was actually lower (0.479 vs 0.498). So the image modality has shown no value so far. It is unclear whether imaging is uninformative or ResNet50 is a weak image encoder. 2. Test: config_036 keeps everything in config_030 fixed (multiprofile, scVI, avgpool, concat) and swaps only ResNet50 for ImageNet ViT-L. This is a one-variable change that isolates the effect of the image encoder within the multimodal setting. 3. Why now: Whether multimodality is worth pursuing is the most important open design decision, because roughly 36 of the remaining configurations are multimodal. If ViT-L gives a clear gain, that strongly supports searching multimodal configurations with ViT-L. 1) Evidence: holding everything else fixed (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool, concat), swapping ResNet50 for ImageNet ViT-L raised validation accuracy from 0.520 to 0.688, with F1 rising from 0.479 to 0.659. The ResNet50 multimodal model only matched RNA-only (0.520 accuracy). So the image encoder looks like the dominant factor, but we don't know how much RNA adds once ViT-L features are present. 2) Test: config_014 is image-only ViT-L with the same multiprofile avgpool setup. It is a clean ablation of the best run with the RNA branch removed. If it scores near 0.69, RNA adds little, and remaining budget should go to image-side and aggregation choices rather than RNA encoders (pca, scGPT) or fusion. If it scores clearly lower, multimodal fusion is synergistic, and RNA encoder and fusion variants with ViT-L become worth exploring. 3) Why now: the RNA encoder and fusion options make up much of the remaining space. A single controlled ablation tells us whether those dimensions deserve budget, which reduces uncertainty more efficiently than an incremental variant of the current best.

Evidence: the image encoder is the dominant factor so far. With scVI RNA, avgpool and concat fusion, swapping ResNet50 for ViT-L raised accuracy from 0.520 to 0.688, and F1 rose with it. The ViT-L multimodal model also beat ViT-L image-only (0.586), so adding RNA helps when paired with a strong image encoder. Aggregation, fusion type and RNA encoder are all still untested, and aggregation has only been tried as avgpool. Test: config_038 keeps the best setup (scVI, ViT-L, multiprofile, concat) and changes only aggregation to transformer. This cleanly isolates whether learned multiprofile aggregation beats mean pooling. Why now: it builds on the strongest result while resolving a major structural choice that affects every multiprofile configuration. Aggregation is likely a larger lever than concat versus weighted fusion. Fusion and RNA encoder can then be tested on whichever aggregation wins.

1) Evidence: imagenet_vit_l clearly beats resnet50 in multimodal concat (0.688 vs 0.520). Multimodal beats either single modality (0.688 vs 0.586 image-only and 0.520 RNA-only). Transformer aggregation slightly beats avgpool (0.715 vs 0.688, with F1 agreeing). The fusion method is completely untested: every multimodal run so far used concat. 2) This run changes only concat to weighted fusion on the current best setup (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + transformer, multiprofile). 1) Evidence: scGPT beats scVI clearly in multimodal concat with ResNet50 (0.579 vs 0.536 multiprofile). Concat beats weighted fusion, and ResNet50 beats ViT-L. 1. Evidence: scGPT with resnet50 and concat fusion is clearly the strongest combination so far (0.586 accuracy single-profile, 0.579 multi-profile avgpool). With scVI, transformer pooling (0.525) was only slightly below avgpool (0.536), a difference too small to draw conclusions from. 2. Test: config_044 keeps the best encoders and fusion fixed (scGPT + resnet50 + concat, multi-profile) and swaps only avgpool for transformer aggregation. 1. No experiments have been run, so every design choice is uncertain: modality, single vs. multiple profiles, RNA encoder, image encoder, aggregation and fusion. 2. Evidence: only one run exists, the multimodal scVI + ViT-L model with avgpool and concat fusion (acc 0.421, F1 0.412). So we have a baseline but no information on which design choice drives it. Evidence: Adding ViT-L image features through concat fusion (config_036, acc 0.421, F1 0.412) performed much worse than RNA-only with the same scVI encoder and avgpool aggregation (config_005, acc 0.535, F1 0.519). 1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_031 (scVI + ResNet50, avgpool, weighted fusion; 0.715 accuracy, 0.687 F1). Several patterns are fairly consistent. 1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_031 (scVI + ResNet50, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted fusion; accuracy 0.715, F1 0.687). 1) No experiments have been run yet, so we have no evidence about which design choice matters most: modality, single- versus multi-profile, RNA encoder, image encoder, aggregation or fusion. 2) This config is a mid-complexity multimodal anchor: scVI RNA features, ResNet50 image features, multi-profile avgpool aggregation and simple concat fusion. Evidence: the multimodal baseline (config_030, scVI + ResNet50, avgpool, concat) reached 0.715 accuracy and 0.687 F1. That is far above RNA-only (0.421) and image-only (0.260) with the same encoders and aggregation. So the multimodal search space is clearly the place to focus. 1. Evidence: The multimodal scVI + ResNet50 + avgpool + concat setup (config_030, acc 0.715, F1 0.687) far exceeds RNA-only (0.421) and image-only (0.260). Aggregation is likely a high-impact design choice in a multiprofile setup and applies across every multimodal branch. 1) Evidence: the best result so far is config_030 (scVI + ResNet50 + avgpool + concat + multiprofile) at 0.715 accuracy and 0.687 F1. Single-factor changes from it have mostly hurt. Evidence: the multimodal multiprofile setup with resnet50 and concat fusion is clearly the strongest region. scvi_n200 with avgpool reached 0.715 (F1 0.687), and the transformer variant was nearly tied at 0.706. pca_n2000 with avgpool was competitive at 0.678. Weighted fusion, singleprofile, scGPT and ViT-L have all done clearly worse, so those directions look unpromising. The open question is whether aggregation interacts with the RNA encoder. It completes a 2x2 comparison of RNA encoder (scvi vs pca) by aggregation (avgpool vs transformer) under the best fusion and image encoder. What this tests: config_018 sets a central reference point. Concat fusion scored only 0.260 and 0.222, and the RNA-only baseline scored 0.422 and 0.405. Aggregation is still completely untested: every run so far used avgpool. 2) This experiment keeps the best configuration (config_031) and changes only the aggregation from avgpool to transformer. That isolates whether learned attention-based pooling across profiles beats simple averaging. 3) It exploits the strongest direction found so far while answering a key open design question with a clean one-factor comparison. The answer will guide whether later experiments on image encoders (vit_l) or RNA encoders (scGPT) should use transformer or avgpool aggregation.

1. Evidence: all four runs so far use the scVI RNA encoder with ResNet50 images. Within that setup, weighted fusion clearly beat concat (0.540 vs 0.260 accuracy, with F1 agreeing). Avgpool beat transformer aggregation under weighted fusion (0.540 vs 0.427). Only the weighted/avgpool multimodal model beat the scVI RNA-only baseline (0.422); concat fell well below it, so fusion design is critical. The image encoder is still completely untested. 2. Evidence: the best result so far is config_037 (scVI + ViT-L, avgpool, weighted fusion; acc 0.579, F1 0.563). Under a limited budget it does two jobs at once: it exploits the strongest known setup and resolves the largest remaining uncertainty, with a realistic chance of a new best result.

Evidence: all six experiments used the multiprofile setting. Within multiprofile, weighted fusion clearly beat concat (0.540 vs 0.260 with scvi/resnet50). Avgpool beat transformer aggregation (0.540 vs 0.427). ImageNet ViT-L beat ResNet50 (0.579 vs 0.540), and scVI beat scGPT (0.579 vs 0.532). The best result so far is config_037 (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, weighted). Test: config_035 keeps the best encoders and weighted fusion but switches to singleprofile. Compared directly with config_037, it isolates the effect of profile setting. Why now: this answers a first-order design question with one experiment. If singleprofile is competitive or better, aggregation choices may matter less and a whole branch of the search space opens. If it is clearly worse, we can confidently focus the remaining budget on multiprofile refinements, such as testing the pca_n2000 RNA encoder.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_037 (scVI + ViT-L, avgpool, weighted fusion), at 0.579 accuracy and 0.563 F1. Other comparisons point the same way. Weighted fusion beats concat. Avgpool beats transformer aggregation. scVI beats scGPT and PCA. Multiprofile beats singleprofile. The open gap is the image side: we have an RNA-only baseline (0.422) but no image-only baseline, so we cannot tell how much of the multimodal gain comes from the ViT-L image features versus true fusion. 2. This experiment tests ViT-L image-only with multiprofile avgpool, matching the best configuration minus RNA. 1) Evidence: The best result so far is image-only ViT-L with avgpool (0.591 accuracy, 0.573 F1). The matching multimodal scVI+ViT-L weighted model is slightly lower (0.579). 1) Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been run, so we have no information about any design choice. That includes the most important one: whether multimodal fusion beats a single modality, and whether pooling over multiple profiles helps. 2) What this tests: config_018 is a multimodal, multiprofile model built from the simplest, cheapest component in each slot: PCA RNA features, ResNet50 image features, average pooling and concatenation fusion. It gives a central anchor point for the search. Later experiments can then change one factor at a time against it, such as dropping a modality, switching to single-profile, using transformer aggregation, weighted fusion, or stronger encoders (scVI/scGPT, ViT-L). 3) Why it is the best first use of the budget: Starting in the middle of the design space lets each later run isolate one factor's effect, which is more efficient than starting at an extreme like an RNA-only, single-profile model. Using plain components avoids confounding early conclusions with sensitivity to complex architectures, while still offering a reasonable chance of strong accuracy.

1. Evidence: Only one experiment exists. The multimodal, multiprofile configuration (PCA RNA, ResNet50 image, avgpool, concat) reached 0.525 accuracy and 0.498 F1. With a single point, we cannot tell which component drives this result, or whether the image branch helps at all. 2. Test: config_002 keeps every other setting the same (PCA, multiprofile, avgpool) but removes the image modality. This is a clean one-factor ablation of the most consequential choice, multimodal versus RNA-only. 3. Why now: Whether to use multimodal models decides which half of the search space is worth exploring. Answering this first is more informative than adjusting aggregation, fusion or encoders within a direction we have not yet validated. Evidence: the multimodal PCA+ResNet50 avgpool concat model (0.525 accuracy, 0.498 F1) beats the matched RNA-only model (0.435, 0.423) by about 9 points. That is a sizeable margin, so the image modality appears to add real signal, and further search should focus on the multimodal space. Uncertainty: the choice of image encoder (ResNet50 vs ImageNet ViT-L) is untested, and it splits the multimodal space in half. Test: config_024 changes only the image encoder relative to the current best, keeping PCA, multiprofile, avgpool and concat fixed. Any difference in accuracy or F1 can therefore be attributed to the encoder alone. Why now: this controlled one-factor comparison resolves a high-impact choice that will guide many later experiments. It also has a reasonable chance of improving on the current best. Aggregation, fusion and RNA-encoder choices can be tested next on whichever image backbone wins.

1) Evidence: multimodal fusion beats RNA-only by about 9 accuracy points (0.525 vs 0.435), so multimodality clearly matters. The two image encoders perform almost the same (ResNet50 0.525 vs ViT-L 0.518, with F1 consistent), so that choice looks minor. That isolates whether learned attention over multiple profiles improves on simple mean pooling. 3) Aggregation is the main mechanism for using multiprofile data and could plausibly have a large effect. The RNA encoder matters: switching from PCA to scGPT gave +0.056 accuracy and +0.040 F1, and scGPT+ResNet50+transformer+concat is the best so far at 0.706. 1) Evidence: Transformer aggregation clearly beats avgpool (0.650 vs 0.525 with PCA+ResNet50). scGPT is the strongest RNA encoder so far (0.706 vs 0.650 for PCA and 0.494 for scVI). 1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_044 (scGPT + ResNet50 + transformer + concat, acc 0.706, F1 0.667). Transformer aggregation clearly beats avgpool (PCA: 0.525 to 0.650). ResNet50 has beaten ViT-L in both paired comparisons. Fusion is the main open question. Weighted fusion has been tried only once (config_045), where it collapsed to 0.328 accuracy and 0.288 F1. That one result could mean weighted fusion is inherently poor, or it could be a failure specific to scGPT, such as an optimization problem. 2) This experiment: config_021 is the strong PCA + ResNet50 + transformer setting (config_020, concat, 0.650), with only the fusion changed to weighted. That makes it a clean paired test of whether weighted fusion fails across RNA encoders. If it collapses again, weighted fusion can be dropped. If it matches or beats concat, the scGPT result was a specific failure, and weighted fusion should be revisited for the best setup. 3) Why now: weighted fusion configurations make up roughly half of the remaining multimodal options. Settling this question, which so far rests on a single run, prunes or reopens the largest share of the search space for one experiment. That is better value than a small exploitative tweak to the current best.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: Several design choices now have consistent evidence. Transformer aggregation beats avgpool (0.650 vs 0.525 with PCA+ResNet50). Concat fusion beats weighted in both pairs tested, and weighted fusion collapsed with scGPT (0.328 vs 0.706). ResNet50 beats ViT-L under both PCA and scGPT. scGPT+ResNet50+transformer+concat (config_044) is the clear best at 0.706 accuracy and 0.667 F1. The profile setting is a major design axis that has never been varied: every run so far used multiprofile. 2. What this tests: config_040 keeps the best encoder pair (scGPT RNA, ResNet50 image) and concat fusion but switches to singleprofile, which has no aggregation. Comparing it with config_044 shows how much of the top result comes from using multiple profiles plus learned transformer aggregation, rather than from the encoders alone. 3. Why it is the best use of the budget: Further tuning of fusion or image encoder around the best config adds little information, since those axes already show consistent direction. A single-axis ablation of a completely untested factor, anchored to the best known configuration, reduces the largest remaining uncertainty. It also clarifies whether multiprofile is essential or whether simpler singleprofile models are competitive.
